# Epistle of Barnabas — Chapter 7 (SOPHIA Consensus)

**Source:** Codex Sinaiticus, Epistle of Barnabas 7
**Agent:** SOPHIA (Consensus)
**Date:** 2026-03-17

---

## Consensus Translation

1. Understand therefore, children of joy, that the good Lord revealed everything to us beforehand, that we might know to whom we should render thanks and praise for all things.
2. If therefore the Son of God — who is Lord and is about to judge the living and the dead — suffered so that his wound might give us life, let us believe that the Son of God was not able to suffer except on our behalf.
3. But also when he was crucified, he was given vinegar and gall to drink. Hear how the priests of the temple provided a type of this: the commandment having been written, "Whoever does not observe the fast shall die the death," the Lord commanded this because he himself was about to offer the vessel of the Spirit as a sacrifice for our sins — so that the type established in Isaac, who was offered upon the altar, might also be fulfilled.
4. What then does he say in the prophet? "And let them eat of the goat offered on the day of the fast for all our sins." Mark carefully: "And let all the priests alone eat the entrails, unwashed with vinegar."
5. Why? "Because I am about to offer my flesh for the sins of my new people, you are going to give me gall and vinegar to drink; therefore you alone shall eat, while the people fast and mourn in sackcloth and ashes" — in order to show that he must suffer at their hands.
6. Mark what was commanded: "Take two goats, fine and equal, and offer them, and let the priest take the one as a whole burnt offering for sins."
7. But what shall they do with the other? "The other," he says, "is accursed." Observe how the type of Jesus is presented here.
8. "And all of you shall spit upon it, and goad it, and bind scarlet wool around its head, and so let it be cast out into the desert." And when this is done, the bearer carries the goat into the wilderness, removes the wool, and places it on the bush called rachia — the shrub from whose shoots we eat when we find them in the field, for the fruit is sweet.
9. Thus I understand: when they shall see him on that day, his long scarlet robe reaching to his feet, they will say, "Is not this the one whom we crucified, despising and piercing him, and spitting upon him? In truth, this was the Son of God."
10. For in the same way he will be like them — and they will not be like him in glory.

---

## Council Notes

- vv.3-9: The Yom Kippur two-goat ritual (Leviticus 16) is given a full christological typology. The two goats = Christ's two appearances (first coming in humility, second in glory). The scarlet wool on the scapegoat = the scarlet robe at the Second Coming. The gall and vinegar = the Passion. Isaac = type of the sacrifice.
- v.8: The rachia bush detail is botanically puzzling and may be a scribal corruption; Barnabas may be thinking of the acacia or a similar desert plant. The sweetness of the fruit may symbolize the ultimate sweetness of Christ's victory.
- v.9: The parousia vision of the condemned seeing Christ in his true identity is a powerful eschatological image; cf. Zechariah 12:10 / Revelation 1:7.
- v.3: "Vessel of the Spirit" — an unusual term for Christ's body; it emphasizes the Spirit's presence in the incarnate Christ, consistent with the two-nature theology developing in this period.
